story_text.value:
I was finding that managing multiple agent threads with walls of text was getting tiring and inefficient for me and that I wanted a more visual way to interact with my agents, so I built Lynx.

Lynx lets you quickly build fully custom interfaces connected to your data sources (e.g. via MCP or API) and trigger agents running on your machine from them (e.g. with Claude Code or Codex).

I built it as an experiment but have found myself doing 80-90% of my work from inside Lynx. I have my own Conductor-like workspace for coding, a Mail client, a workspace for my writing, and various others for dashboards and explorations.

A few things are really cool about it:

- Adding buttons to a UI that trigger a Claude Code agent running on my machine (e.g. to review a PR, get started on a task from Linear, or look for typos in my text)

- Iterating on the interfaces is really easy, particularly because of a point tool that let's you select what you want changed and an agent will update it live

- Switching between workspaces takes a fraction of a second (much faster than e.g. switching between websites)

- It's all local :)

Harnesses have been moving towards native support for artifacts and MCP-UI which kind of go in this direction but I think the current models add to context fragmentation rather than actually help it, so I flipped the model on its head and built an AI workspace / harness where interactive interfaces are at the core.

Calling this an AI workspace for now but honestly unsure what the proper term should be. Is this a visual harness? A hub for personal software?

Keen to hear feedback about the conceptual model and what others have done that might be similar!

title.value: Show HN: Lynx – open-source fully-customizable AI workspace

I’ve had acne for 10 years and I'm so exhausted of dont know what happened. 
So, I'm building AcneAlly to learn you overtime to figure out what's causing your acne, and to give personalized support. 
Instead of  tracking your skin or logging daily habits, you can just talk or interact with it like a companion. You can share about your acne, share your concerns, or ask anything you want. Based on what you share, it uses Al to reasoning to make guesses about what could be causing your acne. As you share more, it update it understanding abt you, its guesses abt the cause and it suggestions.
This is an early version, and there's still a lot to improve.
I'd love to hear your feedback!
Thanks for checking it out!

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I’m Eric and I’m building Lettercamp, an open-source static blog framework. The repo is at https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and the homepage is online at https://www.lettercamp.com.

Writing good content has always been the #1 way that I’ve grown the reach of products I’ve worked on in the past. However, it’s always bothered me how many little things get in the way of writing and publishing high quality, first party content onto the web.

Building a performant, SEO-optimized blog from scratch was always distracting from development on the actual product, and setting up a 3rd party CMS meant that my content always lived in someone else’s database. Storing content in a non-markdown format also made it difficult to draft and edit with the help of an AI agent.

Lettercamp is a modern approach to creating a content site. It ships with all the little features you’d expect in a blog: pagination, authors, metadata, search, cross linking, related posts and more. It’s also statically built, which means that all your content lives in markdown in your codebase, so a deployed version is performant with no database to maintain. This means that you can focus on writing good content instead of vibe-coding a whole blog.

I want to add more features to the framework over time, including better support for AI agents, built in localization, email sign ups, and more.

The repo is released under the MIT license so that anyone can use the framework to create a content site. The goal isn’t to charge individual developers. The monetization path is to provide a cloud hosted version, that has an online editor that content teams can use. The main advantage of this is to decouple the blog from product deploys, so that teams can publish content without needing to push code.

I would love to get your feedback on if this is a problem that might resonate with you or your team. I know that a lot of products create a /blog section at some point, and I wonder what solutions people are using today. My hope is that over time, Lettercamp can be the go-to solution for teams looking to set this up.

Try it out: https://github.com/lettercamp/lettercamp and let me know what you think!

story_text.value:
Just released Zumungo AI driven Home Automation zumungo.com. Zumungo uses the power and flexibility of well established open source projects such as HomeAssitant, Frigate, Whisper, go2rtc, Piper, Open AI, Ollama, etc. It wraps everything in easy to use user interface for non professional users. In addition Zumungo allows users to add their own devices that are not part of the catalog. Of course Zumungo is full blown Home Automation platform and has build-in servers for managing all IoT protocols such as Matter, Thread, Zigbee, Zwave, MQTT, BT, TCP, mDNS etc.

Special attention is paid to security and camera management all the way to implementing Vision AI. In my tests Zumungo announces "UPS truck approaching the drive way. A person carrying a package walks towards the door". This announcement is processed by an event and results in "UPS delivery" on the GH speakers around the house.

Zumungo has it's own event engine that is easy to use by both the user as well as AI Agent. User can tell AI agent " Create an event to open the garage door and turn on the porch light, upon my arrival home on foot or by car tracked by zumungo geo fencing".

Option exist for users to design their own panels to display on tablets on the wall or desktop computers for even easier management of the house by family members, guests, kids etc. For example if you rent your ADU on Airbnb than you can create dedicated panel on a tablet for guests to use that controls their rooms only and has no access to the main house.

Zumungo has it's own mobile app available at iOS store. For Android devices it is downloadable from Zumungo server itself.

As far as AI goes, Zumungo offers simple interface in settings for user to pick and choose online AI agent from the major 3 ( Claude, Gemini or Open AI ) or pick a local agent from a list of various agents. Available local agents include Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Phi and others. Zumungo always updates the agents to the best and latest and always vets them for licensing and legal compliance. Zumungo also advises user what kind of hardware is needed for particular agent to run typically 16GB or more of GPU memory.

Trying Zumngo is easy. One line on any Linux machine or ready made RPi image - download-flash and go. See "get started" at Zumungo web site.

Support issues come after trying and this is taken care of as well at Zumungo Forums or just email support@zumungo.com

story_text.value:
Background: I've been working on Sporadic for years, while software engineering has been my full-time job. That means this code is mine, and I know it well since it was built in the pre-AI era. However, AI has allowed me to expand the features to a place where I am more confident in sharing it.

Why: As an engineer, I sit and look at a screen all day. My brother is a graphic designer and does the same. Our goal was to build an app to get us on our feet, and one where we could do it together. What makes Sporadic fun is a mix of short exercises at random times during your day that you can do with your friends. We've got stats, streaks, and community-wide daily challenges. The mix of social accountability, random timing of challenges, and a streak to hold onto make it an effective tool for convincing me to do some push-ups between meetings.

How it works: Get a push notification to do a specific short exercise within a given time limit. These can also be done with friends, and you'll get a push when they complete one. A buddy doing the challenge is an incredible motivator.

Tech: I started this project long ago to learn Swift and SwiftUI. The project is decidedly Apple, with a CloudKit database on the back end. One really cool thing this gives me is the ability to have an authenticated user based on their iCloud account only, so you don't have to create an account to use Sporadic and join up with friends. Otherwise, CloudKit is pretty frustrating to use, and it will make it more difficult to add support for Android. If there is any Android demand, please let me know!

Conclusion: I've enjoyed using Sporadic myself and hope that someone else out there could benefit from it. I would love some feedback on what is good and what needs improved. Thanks for reading.
